title: Attacks, services and defenses
covers: Passive vs active attacks, security services & mechanisms, OSI security architecture, network security model
learningGoals: You will be able to classify attacks as passive eavesdropping or active tampering.
You will be able to map security services to matching cryptographic mechanisms.
You will be able to explain the OSI X.800 security architecture.

lessonCards.title: Passive vs Active Attacks
lessonCards.analogy: A passive wiretapper listens to phone calls silently. An active attacker impersonates the caller.
lessonCards.coreConcept: Passive attacks eavesdrop without altering data (hard to detect, easy to prevent). Active attacks modify, replay, or fabricate packets.
lessonCards.example: Packet sniffing Wi-Fi traffic is passive; sending counterfeit DNS packets is active.

lessonCards.title: X.800 Security Services
lessonCards.analogy: A courier service offers locked boxes (encryption), stamped wax seals (integrity), and photo ID (authentication).
lessonCards.coreConcept: X.800 defines five service classes: Authentication, Access Control, Data Confidentiality, Data Integrity, and Non-repudiation.
lessonCards.example: Signing a PDF contract provides non-repudiation so the signer cannot deny sending it.

lessonCards.title: Network Security Model
lessonCards.analogy: Two castles send secret envoys across bandit-patrolled wilderness using trusted secret keys.
lessonCards.coreConcept: A message is transformed by a security algorithm using a secret key, transmitted across an insecure channel, and verified at the destination.
lessonCards.example: Your browser encrypts passwords with TLS before sending them across public coffee-shop Wi-Fi.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is classified as a PASSIVE network attack?
questions.explanation: Traffic analysis observes transmission patterns without altering message contents.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Eavesdropping without modifying data is passive.
Altering packets actively manipulates data.
Replaying captured packets introduces active network traffic.
Flooding servers actively degrades availability.
questions.realWorldExample: Eavesdroppers on unencrypted public Wi-Fi inspect packet traffic with Wireshark.

questions.prompt: Under the X.800 architecture, what does Non-Repudiation prevent?
options: A sender falsely denying they sent a message
An eavesdropper from stealing a password
A web browser from rendering HTML
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation provides indisputable cryptographic proof that a specific party originated a message.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Digital signatures provide proof of origin that cannot be credibly denied.
Hardware faults are handled by RAID redundancy.
Confidentiality prevents eavesdropping.
Browser rendering is presentation.
questions.realWorldExample: Financial wire transfers require cryptographic digital signatures to legally prove origin.

questions.prompt: Why are passive attacks generally harder to detect than active attacks?
options: Because passive attacks do not alter data or create transmission errors
Because passive attackers always use supercomputers
Because passive attacks delete log files immediately
Because routers do not process passive packets
questions.explanation: Since passive attacks merely observe data without modifying bits, they leave zero detectable file or network footprint.
wrongExplanations: Correct! No altered bits means no error logs or integrity alerts are triggered.
Passive sniffing can be executed on cheap hardware taps.
Passive eavesdroppers do not possess server write access.
Routers route packets normally.
questions.realWorldExample: Fiber-optic cable tapping copies light pulses without interrupting traffic.

questions.prompt: An attacker captures a user's login packet and resends it minutes later to authenticate. What attack is this?
questions.explanation: A replay attack re-transmits valid intercepted authentication messages to gain unauthorized access.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Capturing and replaying valid credentials is a classic active replay attack.
DoS takes systems down.
Traffic analysis only examines timing frequencies.
Cryptanalysis breaks mathematical ciphers.
questions.realWorldExample: Car key fob relay attacks record unlock radio signals to unlock vehicle doors later.

questions.prompt: Which cryptographic mechanism is the primary defense against passive eavesdropping?
questions.explanation: Encryption scrambles plaintext into ciphertext, rendering intercepted data unreadable to passive listeners.
wrongExplanations: Correct! Strong encryption renders eavesdropped bytes meaningless to the attacker.
Checksums verify integrity but do not hide information.
Packet counters measure bandwidth.
Port knocking hides ports.
questions.realWorldExample: HTTPS TLS 1.3 prevents ISPs from reading credit card numbers submitted in web forms.

questions.prompt: In the standard network security model, what trusted component is responsible for distributing secret keys?
questions.explanation: A Trusted Third Party (such as a KDC or Certificate Authority) validates identities and distributes cryptographic keys.
wrongExplanations: Correct! A trusted authority securely issues or certifies public and private credentials.
Public routers are untrusted intermediate hops.
Standard DNS resolves names without guaranteeing key secrecy.
The adversary is the hostile entity.
questions.realWorldExample: Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) Certificate Authorities like Let's Encrypt issue web domain certificates.

ashRecap: Passive attacks eavesdrop quietly, while active attacks alter the conversation. Encryption shields you against both!
